analysis.one_liner: Taxes every stock, bond, and derivatives trade, with the rate rising to 0.1%, to raise federal revenue from high-volume trading.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would put a tax of up to 0.1% on financial trades, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small federal tax on every purchase of stocks, most bonds, and derivatives contracts — financial contracts whose value is tied to stocks, bonds, commodities, currencies, or indexes. The tax starts at 0.02% of the trade's value in 2026 and rises to 0.1% by 2030. Stock exchanges and brokers would collect it on each trade, and the rules reach foreign subsidiaries of US firms to prevent trades being routed overseas to dodge the tax. Buying a newly issued stock or bond is exempt, as are insurance contracts, most hedging by commodities businesses, and very short-term government-style debt. The bill says nothing about how the money raised would be spent.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, the federal government would gain a new revenue stream funded by a levy on securities trading. Because the tax is charged per trade, its relative burden falls heaviest on high-frequency traders and large financial institutions, not on anyone's paycheck. The bill text does not earmark the revenue, so any benefit to ordinary people would depend on Congress later deciding to spend it on, say, deficit reduction or public programs. To the extent the tax discourages rapid-fire speculative trading, markets could see somewhat less of it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers, if revenue is spent well

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a federal tax on each covered trade — stocks, bonds (except very short-term debt of 100 days or less), and derivatives — starting at 0.02% and rising to 0.1% of the trade's value by 2030, generating federal revenue paid mostly by financial institutions and heavy traders rather than by wages or consumer purchases.

The tax applies even when the trading is routed through a foreign subsidiary, since US-owned foreign corporations are treated as US persons and their US owners must pay the tax, limiting the industry's ability to sidestep it by moving trades offshore.

The Secretary of the Treasury is directed to write rules to prevent avoidance, including rules covering the use of non-US persons in the transactions, and to run the tax in consultation with the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

analysis.who_pays: The cost lands on anyone who buys stocks, bonds, or derivatives — exchanges and US brokers must collect the tax on each trade and pass it through. Individual investors saving for retirement would pay a small amount per purchase (0.1% of a $10,000 stock purchase is $10), while firms trading billions daily would bear the bulk of the money raised in absolute terms. Costs embedded in derivatives and hedging could filter into prices throughout the financial system.

drawbacks.text: Every purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative — including by mutual funds and index funds held in retirement accounts — carries the tax, which brokers and exchanges collect and pass on, so ordinary investors' trading costs would rise slightly and fund returns would dip a bit.

The bill creates a new revenue stream but contains no provision directing how the money would be used, so there is no guarantee in the text itself that the proceeds would fund anything benefiting ordinary people.

A tax on every trade makes it marginally more expensive to buy and sell securities, which could slightly reduce market liquidity — the ease with which investors can get in and out of positions — a cost that touches retirement savers, not just big traders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but contingent: a small tax on high-volume securities trading raises meaningful revenue with the burden falling mostly on financial firms rather than on wages or consumer purchases, and it might modestly dampen the most speculative short-term trading. The costs are that every investor who buys a stock — including someone putting money into an index fund in a 401(k) — pays a little more per purchase, that easy-to-trade markets become somewhat more expensive for everyone, and that the bill never says what the money would be used for, so the benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on decisions Congress has not made. Overall a straightforward progressive tax whose design is reasonable but whose public payoff is undefined in the text itself.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it sits there with no vote in sight.

narrative.text: Introduced June 18, 2025, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, the standard first step for a tax bill.
The action history ends there: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action has been scheduled.
The bill would tax most securities trades at rates phasing from 0.02% up to 0.1% of the trade's value, with exchanges and brokers responsible for collecting it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the securities industry, which would bear the tax, is better off: the bill has not moved out of committee, and no trading costs have changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms, for now

for.name: Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and serves as its lead sponsor.

for.name: 5 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Warren, Van Hollen, Whitehouse, Fetterman, Merkley)

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, took no action on it — no hearing or markup appears in the record after the June 2025 referral.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats, and with Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and chairing the Finance Committee, the bill has no path to a vote without Republican support, which the record does not show.

industries.industry: High-frequency trading and securities trading firms
industries.note: These firms make money on enormous numbers of trades with tiny margins per trade; a tax of up to 0.1% on every trade falls hardest on them. That cost is the bill's main point. For ordinary people this is where the revenue comes from, so the industry's interest runs against the bill's purpose.

industries.industry: Wall Street banks and investment firms
industries.note: Banks pay the tax on their own trading and pass some of it to clients, but the exemptions for hedging, dealer financing, and inter-affiliate trades soften the hit. The net effect is a new cost on their trading businesses.

Exchanges and US brokers are made responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on every trade they handle, adding compliance machinery, while the tax itself raises transaction costs for their customers. Retail investors would feel this as slightly higher trading costs.
Insurance, annuity, and endowment contracts are expressly excluded from the definition of a taxable derivative, so these companies and their products sit outside the tax.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 of 100 Senate seats and the Finance chairmanship, a financial transaction tax has essentially no path to a markup or floor vote this Congress. The most likely outcome is that it stays in committee and dies when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, as similar proposals have before; reintroduction in a future Congress would depend on control of the Senate changing.
